newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH SENATE RUNOFF DIVIDES GOVERNING COALITION.
newsitem.headline: CZECH SENATE RUNOFF DIVIDES GOVERNING COALITION.

text.p: The three-party Czech ruling coalition showed deep fissures on Tuesday in a dispute over supporting each others' candidates in second-round runoff elections to the new Senate this weekend.

Prime Minisiter Vaclav Klaus who leads the senior Civic Democratic Party (ODS) on Tuesday labelled the refusal of the heads of the two junior parties in the centre-right coalition to give blanket support to ODS candidates as "scandalous".

"I ... take it as scandalous that we did not manage to find a common voice which would say to voters... that even though we have different views on minor issues, our opinion on the future of this Senate is the same," Klaus told a news conference.

The coalition Christian Democratic Union (KDU-CSL) and Civic Democratic Aliance (ODA) both said -- after ODS put 76 candidates in second-round runoffs out of 81 constiutencies -- it was up to local party leaders to endorse whom they wanted.

Both KDU-CSL chairman Josef Lux and ODA chief Jan Kalvoda, each a vice-premier, criticised Klaus and his party for directly appealing to unsuccessful first round candidates from each party to back ODS candidates in the second round.
Lux said Klaus acted "scandalously" by contacting individual candidates personally and going over the heads of the coalition parties' leadership in Prague.
"Everyone is learning democracy, including the prime minister," Lux told a rally in the Czech capital on Tuesday.
The Czech agency CTK quoted Kalvoda as saying Klaus "violated political culture" through his tactics.
The three-party conservative coalition, dominated by ODS, has had a series of internal spats since forming in 1992, but the group remains the longest-serving post-Communist government in Europe.

ODS candidates won three seats outright in last weekend's first round by getting more than 50 percent of the vote in their constituency, and 73 candidates took the most votes in their district going into the runoff.

The strongest opposition party, the Social Democrats who took away the coalition's majority in the lower house with a better than expected result in June elections, put only 48 candidates in the Senate runoffs, and won no seats outright.

The centre-left Social Democrats have said they would rather their supporters, in districts where they did not have a candidate in the runoff on Friday and Saturdy, would support any candidate, except those from ODS.

ODS representatives have tried to convice Czech voters the Social Democrats position on endorsements implied closer cooperation with the KSCM, which they say threatens to throw the country back to its Communist past.

"CSSD ... must finally make up its mind whether it wants to be a state-building party... or whether all it wants is to grab power along with the Communists," Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec, one of the ODS's more moderate critics of CSSD, told a news conference.
